Unified Service

AI that assists. Never insists.

Aurora OS re-engineers how applications communicate with intelligence. By centralizing reasoning into an OS-level service, your computer stays quiet, fast, and unified.

  • Unified system service: Applications share a single, optimized intelligence provider.
  • Pluggable model backends: Use local neural weights or tiny fast SLMs without rewriting apps.
  • Predictable resilience: If an AI model stalls, the Linux desktop never crashes.

Strict Confinement

Your thoughts are yours alone.

In an era where desktop operating systems take silent screenshots of your activity and push background telemetry, Aurora OS stands as an unyielding fortress for your personal privacy.

  • Zero background telemetry: What happens on your silicon stays on your silicon.
  • Linux openat2 sandboxing: Resolves files strictly beneath user directories with zero symlink traversal.
  • Default-deny policy: Unpermitted capabilities are blocked in 0.14 ms.

Performance Baselines

Sub-millisecond. Because waiting is a relic.

Operating system services should be invisible until you need them. Built in Rust with asynchronous Tokio pipelines and anonymous socketpair communication, Aurora OS delivers incredible performance.

  • 0.061 ms median turn latency: Over 15,000 sustained capability turns per second.
  • Zero memory creep: The core daemon maintains a flat resident set size (VmRSS).
  • 100% test pass rate: 211 automated test suites passing with zero regressions.

Engineering Foundation

Linux underneath. Pure stability.

We did not attempt to build a custom kernel from scratch. Linux already provides three decades of engineering in process management, filesystems, hardware drivers, and memory security.

  • Total hardware compatibility: Runs on laptops, desktops, and workstations effortlessly.
  • Standard desktop software: Run Steam, Flatpak, Docker, VS Code, and standard Linux apps natively.
  • Modern POSIX userspace: Built around systemd, standard POSIX APIs, and open standards.

Security Invariants

Zero ambient authority. Built from the ground up.

Applications never receive automatic system-wide surveillance powers. Every capability requires an explicit, cryptographically checked token. If an action isn't permitted, the request fails closed in microseconds.

AVX-512 & Intel AMX Matrix Engines

Aurora OS incorporates specialized vector dispatch routines that dynamically detect AVX-512 (F, CD, BW, DQ, VL) and Intel Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX). On CPUs with AMX tiles, 8-bit quantized matrix multiplication achieves up to 3.2× higher throughput than standard AVX2, enabling responsive 8B models without requiring a discrete graphics card.

Dedicated Linux NPU Subsystems (XDNA 2 & VPU)

Modern Neural Processing Units (NPUs) are treated as first-class asynchronous accelerators. Through the upstream Linux amdgpu_xdna and intel_vpu drivers, the aurora-ai daemon delegates lightweight audio transcription (Whisper) and semantic vector embeddings (BGE) to the NPU at sub-15W power consumption, preserving the discrete GPU for primary reasoning tasks.

CUDA vs ROCm vs oneAPI Level Zero

Aurora OS provides a vendor-neutral capability dispatcher. The internal daemon dynamically negotiates compute jobs across CUDA (for NVIDIA Tensor Cores), ROCm HIP (for AMD Matrix Cores), and Level Zero (for Intel XMX engines), utilizing native hardware intrinsics while providing unified, zero-overhead D-Bus abstractions to desktop applications.

Open-Source Kernel Modules (`nvidia-open` & `amdgpu`)

We prioritize open-source kernel drivers for stability and security. Modern NVIDIA Ada cards utilize the MIT/GPL nvidia-open kernel module, AMD hardware runs through upstream amdgpu and ROCm, and Intel utilizes the open xe and i915 drivers, guaranteeing no proprietary binary blobs reside in the core kernel memory space.

The Memory Bandwidth Wall Explained

Autoregressive language models generate tokens sequentially. To predict each single token, the entire active model weight matrix must be transferred from memory into compute execution units. While prompt evaluation (prefill) is compute-bound, token generation is almost exclusively memory bandwidth bound. A system with 500 GB/s bandwidth can generate an 8B Q4 model (~5 GB) at roughly 75 tokens per second.

KV Cache Footprint at Extended Context Lengths

As conversation and code context grows (from 4k tokens to 32k or 128k tokens), the Key-Value (KV) cache grows linearly in memory. Aurora OS incorporates FlashAttention-2 and paged attention in the Tokio worker supervisor to prevent memory fragmentation and compress idle context windows into pinned zero-copy system memory buffers.

Quantization Science: Q4_K_M vs Q8_0 vs FP16

Quantization reduces memory footprint with minimal impact on output quality. Q4_K_M (4-bit medium) achieves over 99.2% of unquantized baseline accuracy while shrinking model size by 68%. For critical code generation and mathematical deduction, Q8_0 (8-bit) preserves absolute precision while fitting comfortably within 12GB to 16GB graphics buffers.

Zero-Copy Host RAM Integration on Linux APUs

Unlike discrete PCIe graphics cards that incur latency copying tensor buffers across bus lanes, modern unified platforms (Apple Silicon via Asahi Linux and AMD Strix Point APUs) share physical memory between CPU and GPU. Aurora OS leverages zero-copy buffer sharing, allowing unified APUs to allocate up to 75% of total system memory directly to inference models.

Questions & Answers

Frequently Asked Questions

Clear answers regarding Aurora OS architecture, privacy principles, compatibility, and licensing.

Is Aurora OS an entirely new kernel or a Linux distribution?

Aurora OS is built directly on top of the standard Linux 6.x kernel. We intentionally chose Linux rather than engineering a kernel from scratch to preserve three decades of battle-tested driver compatibility, robust POSIX file systems, and hardware support across laptops, desktops, and workstations.

Aurora’s innovation lives in its userspace: the lightweight aurora-ai system daemon, hardware-isolated sandboxing, and unified desktop intelligence.

How does Aurora OS protect privacy? Does my data leave my machine?

Privacy in Aurora OS is an architectural guarantee, not merely a policy statement. All conversational contexts, tool invocation parameters, and vector search embeddings reside strictly on your local hardware.

The system daemon operates inside a constrained Linux sandbox using Landlock and seccomp filters. No background telemetry or unsolicited phone-home connections are ever made without explicit, interactive authorization.

Can I run standard Linux software, Steam games, and developer tools?

Yes, 100%. Because Aurora OS is built on the Linux kernel with standard POSIX libraries and Wayland/X11 display protocols, everything you expect on a Linux workstation runs seamlessly out of the box:

  • Productivity & Browsers: Chrome, Firefox, LibreOffice, Slack, Discord.
  • Developer Toolchains: VS Code, Neovim, Docker, Podman, Rust, Python, Go, Node.js.
  • Gaming & Media: Steam, Proton, Lutris, OBS Studio, Blender.
What are the minimum hardware requirements?

Aurora’s core daemon is written in safe Rust with an idle resident memory footprint under 3 MB, meaning it introduces virtually zero overhead to the OS.

  • Base OS: Any modern 64-bit x86_64 or aarch64 processor, 4 GB RAM, 20 GB storage.
  • Local AI Acceleration (Optional): For on-device LLM inference (e.g. 7B/8B models), an integrated NPU or discrete GPU with 8 GB+ VRAM (NVIDIA CUDA, AMD ROCm, or Intel Vulkan) is recommended.
How does Aurora prevent AI agents from harming my files?

We leverage kernel-grade isolation rather than relying on software prompts. All filesystem interactions run through Linux openat2 with RESOLVE_BENEATH and RESOLVE_NO_SYMLINKS flags, making directory escape attacks impossible.

Additionally, tool invocations require deterministic policy evaluation (evaluated in just 0.141 ms), preventing unintended mutations to root or system directories.

Is Aurora OS open source, and how can I contribute?

Aurora OS is entirely free and open-source software licensed under the MIT License. All codebase development, architectural decision records (ADRs), and performance benchmarks are hosted on GitHub.

You can clone the repository, run the test suites with cargo test, submit pull requests, or participate in discussions on the Aurora OS GitHub Repository.
